    Instructor Notes

    These notes are for instructors and helpers. They cover preparation, teaching, timing, checkpoints, feedback, the data and the answer keys. The design record (objectives, report card, assessment map, misconceptions and concept map) is on the Lesson Design page. In the Instructor View, the instructor notes from every episode follow these notes, in episode order.

    The Lesson in One Paragraph

    The lesson makes three passes over one nine-step workflow (data, model, fit, check the fit, estimates, check the model, random effect, compare, forecast). In the first pass you demonstrate on Stellako sockeye salmon. In the second, learners repeat each step on Upper Pitt River in the “Your Turn” challenges, and fill in one row of a model report card per episode. In the third, the Capstone, pairs apply the whole workflow to a stock they choose, or to their own data. The Quick Start runs all nine steps in one hour, and each later episode opens one step as one or more recipe cards. Learners copy each recipe into their own my-recipes.R; the finished recipe box (cookbook.R) holds every recipe, in lesson order.

    Before the Workshop

    • Send the Setup page a week ahead, and ask learners to reply (by email or a form) with the line Your setup works. that the setup check prints.

    • Collect the answers to the three self-check questions on the Setup page. Anyone who gets two of the three wrong should take an introductory R lesson first; tell them before the workshop, kindly.

    • Prepare:

      • sticky notes in two colours that colour-blind learners can tell apart: green for “done” and pink for “I need help” (avoid red and orange, which many colour-blind people cannot tell from green); learners also write a question mark on a help note, so that colour is not the only cue;
      • a shared notes document with a “parking lot” section for questions that a later episode answers;
      • a shared table for the capstone share-out, with the columns listed in the capstone (stock; best by AIC, with the AIC difference to the next; best by hindcast skill; random-walk 80% coverage; do AIC and the hindcast agree?; one sentence);
      • printed copies of the Recipe Index;
      • the link to the code handout (files/code-handout.R on the built site), which holds every recipe chunk.

    • Offer an optional setup help desk at 08:30 on Day 1.

    • Rehearse on the computer you will teach from. In a project with data/ and files/ set up as on the Setup page, run:

      R 

      source("files/quick-start.R")
check_fit(opt, sdr)
check_fit(opt_walk, sdr_walk)
c(ricker = aic(opt), walk = aic(opt_walk))

      It takes about 3 seconds and must print four TRUE twice, then the two AIC values:

      OUTPUT 

       finished      flat    curved finite_se
     TRUE      TRUE      TRUE      TRUE
 finished      flat    curved finite_se
     TRUE      TRUE      TRUE      TRUE
  ricker     walk
198.2570 178.3082

    Teaching

    • Teach by participatory live coding, with a large font and dark text on a light background. Type everything, say each line as you type it, then explain it again.
    • There are three exceptions to typing:
      • learners who fall behind in the Quick Start may paste from the Quick Start script (quick-start.R); the Quick Start is the only episode where learners may paste whole steps;
      • naive_forecast() in Episode 11 is read together, not typed: it comes from source("files/cookbook.R") in the Starting Point, so learners who skipped the Starting Point run that line (or paste the function into my-recipes.R);
      • the capstone uses the capstone template (capstone-template.R).
    • Make the planned mistakes live, and let learners read the output before you explain it:
      • the missing minus sign in front of sum() (Episode 4);
      • the missing random = argument (Episodes 4 and 8);
      • the random-effect vector that is one value too short (Episode 6).
    • Ask “What questions do you have?”, not “Any questions?”. Write deep questions in the parking lot, labelled with the episode that answers them, and come back to them there.
    • Keep to the lesson’s one way per task. If someone asks about another method, say that it exists and point to where the lesson covers it:
      • lm(): the callout “If You Know lm()” in Writing a Model as a Likelihood;
      • Bayesian fitting, REPORT() and formula packages such as glmmTMB: the Going Further page;
      • optim(): nlminb() does the same job, and the lesson uses one optimiser throughout.

    Timing and Cuts

    The time budget, in minutes. The schedule on the home page (Instructor View) is built from the teaching: and exercises: values at the top of each episode, which are these numbers.

    Time budget per episode (minutes) and number of challenges.
    Episode Teaching Exercises Total Challenges
    01 Introduction: Salmon, Spawners and Recruits 15 10 25 2
    02 Quick Start: The Whole Workflow in Nine Steps 40 20 60 6
    03 Writing a Model as a Likelihood 30 25 55 5
    04 Fitting a Model and Checking the Fit 30 25 55 4
    05 Estimates, Intervals and Derived Quantities 30 20 50 4 (+1 optional)
    06 Random Effects: Productivity That Changes over Time 35 25 60 4
    07 Checking a Model with Residuals 25 20 45 3
    Day 1 205 145 350
    08 Checking a Model with Simulation 25 25 50 6
    09 Comparing Models with AIC 35 30 65 5
    10 Many Stocks: Random Effects for Groups (optional) 25 20 45 4
    11 Forecasting and Testing Forecasts 40 35 75 5 (+1 optional)
    12 Capstone: A Model Report for a New Stock 10 80 90 2 (+1 optional)
    Day 2 135 190 325
    Total 340 335 675 50 (+3 optional)
    • Exercises take half of the time. Episodes 1 to 11 have 50 challenges (two of them optional) in 330 minutes of teaching: one every 7 minutes on average.
    • All times are first estimates. After you teach, replace teaching: and exercises: at the top of each episode with the times you measured.

    When you fall behind, never speed up: cut whole pieces, and tell learners where the skipped material is. Cut in this order:

    1. Episode 10 (Many Stocks). Tell the pooled-NPGO story in two minutes at the end of Episode 9: across all 19 stocks, the North Pacific Gyre Oscillation (NPGO) index lowers AIC by 16 without shared year effects, but raises it by 0.6 with them.
    2. In Episode 8, demonstrate the self-test instead of having learners type self_test().
    3. Episode 3, Challenge 2 and Episode 5, Challenge 2.
    4. Episode 11, Challenge 3.
    5. Capstone rows 5 and 6.

    Never cut the Quick Start, Episode 4, the core of Episodes 7, 9 and 11, or capstone rows 2, 3, 7, 8 and 9.

    A workshop can stop at two points and still be useful:

    • after Episode 7: one stock is fitted, reported and checked with residuals (lesson objectives 1 to 4, and the residual part of objective 5);
    • after Episode 9: models can also be compared (objectives 1 to 6).

    Responding to Multiple-Choice Answers

    Every wrong option in a multiple-choice challenge comes from a named misconception. Plan your response before you ask:

    • if most learners pick one wrong answer, re-teach the misconception it names, using the evidence in the table below;
    • if answers are spread out, go back to the last point everyone understood;
    • if almost everyone is right, move on.

    In the table, E03.C2 means Episode 3, Challenge 2.

    Misconceptions, the evidence to re-teach with, and where the lesson targets them.
    # Misconception Evidence (from the lesson’s own runs) Targeted by
    M1 Return the log-likelihood, not its negative opt$convergence is 0 with the message “X-convergence (3)”, opt$objective is -Inf, and the checks are TRUE FALSE FALSE FALSE E03.C2, E04.C1
    M2 convergence == 0 means the fit is usable the same output E04.C1
    M3 If the optimiser finished on flat ground, the standard errors are fine two parameters that do one job: finished TRUE, flat TRUE, every standard error NaN E04.C2
    M4 Back-transform as exp(estimate) ± 1.96 SE gives 122.2 to 123.3 instead of 73 to 207 thousand for Stellako’s S_max E05.C1
    M5 A confidence band should contain most data points the 95% band holds 24% of the Stellako points E05.C3, E11.C1
    M6 exp() of a log-scale forecast is the mean median 148, mean 199 thousand recruits E11.C2
    M7 random = means “draw random numbers”; an SD at zero means the fit failed Harrison: four checks TRUE, sd_walk 5e-6, AIC exactly 2.00 above the Ricker E06.C1, E06.C4
    M8 Observed-minus-fitted residuals are fine for random-effect models conditional residuals have SD 0.96 and lag-1 correlation -0.17; one-step-ahead residuals have SD 1.00 and -0.10 Episode 7 spoiler and keypoint
    M9 Models fitted to different rows can be compared by AIC the Ricker on 1958-2021 has AIC 177.2 and appears to beat the random walk on 1948-2021 (178.3); on the same rows the walk wins by 17.6 E09.C3
    M10 Lower AIC means better forecasts Upper Pitt River: AIC prefers the random walk by 11.8, but the Ricker’s hindcast errors are slightly smaller (skill 0.78 against 0.82); Chilko and Birkenhead in the capstone (AIC and the hindcast choose different models), and Late Stuart (the lowest-AIC model forecasts no better than the recent-average benchmark) E11.C4, capstone share-out
    M11 Changing dat after a fit is harmless with the raw RTMB calls, dat$S_new <- 150 after fitting silently changed sdreport()’s mu_new from 1.97 to 1.16 Episode 4 spoiler (demonstration)
    M12 A covariate that lowers AIC is robust pooled NPGO: AIC changes by -16.0 without year effects and +0.57 with them E10.C4
    M13 An SD estimated at zero proves there is no variation self-test: 11 of 50 data sets simulated with sd_walk 0.13 gave an estimate of about zero E06.C4 (option c), E08.C6
    M14 obj$simulate() without arguments uses the fitted values it uses the parameters evaluated last Episode 8 caution
    M15 S_max is a carrying capacity (terminology) Episode 5 caution
    M16 AIC can compare a model of log(R/S) with a model of R the two models describe different responses E09.C5

    Feedback

    • Collect minute cards at lunch on both days: one thing that went well, and one question or thing that was unclear.
    • Collect one-up/one-down at the end of each day: each learner says one thing to keep and one thing to change.
    • Open Day 2 by saying what you changed after Day 1’s feedback (5 minutes).
    • Day 2 starts with the Parsons warm-up, Checking a Model with Simulation, Challenge 1: it rebuilds Day 1’s fitting recipe and reminds everyone of random =.

    Data Notes

    • Stellako brood year 2005 (102 thousand spawners, 11.6 thousand recruits) returned mainly in 2009, one of the poorest Fraser River sockeye returns on record. It is real; do not delete it. Episode 7, Challenge 3 asks what to do about it.
    • Upper Pitt River is the “Your Turn” stock because it behaves like Stellako but has two differences worth discussing: NPGO helps, and AIC and the hindcast disagree.
    • Harrison is the only stock with brood year 2022, so its hindcast from 2007 has 16 forecasts instead of 15.
    • Quesnel and Late Stuart have strong four-year cycles and years with under 1 thousand spawners (25 years for Quesnel, 9 for Late Stuart). Every fit still passes all four checks, but under the random walk Quesnel’s S_max (3481 thousand) is far beyond its data.
    • Early Stuart (in 2019 and 2020 only 46 and 15 fish spawned: 0.046 and 0.015 thousand) and Late Shuswap (S_max beyond the data) are left out of the examples on purpose.
    • Cultus, Portage and Scotch Creek have missing years. Every recipe handles them, but they are not on the capstone menu.
    • The data were supplied with the Pacific Salmon Commission RTMB workshop and described there as “not necessarily official numbers”. The lesson uses them to teach methods; nothing in it is management advice. These stocks matter to First Nations and to commercial and recreational fisheries: treat questions about them with care, following the CARE principles for Indigenous data governance.

    Hidden Curriculum to Make Explicit

    Say these out loud when they first come up; experienced R users do them without thinking.

    • Work in a project, and use relative paths such as data/sockeye.csv.
    • Keep code in a script, not in the console, so you can rerun it.
    • Read an error message from the bottom up, then find it on the Troubleshooting page.
    • Call set.seed() before anything that simulates, so the numbers can be reproduced.
    • Save report-card.R as you go: each row is written as soon as its challenge runs.
    • Use new object names in your own experiments (ricker_test, not ricker), so you do not overwrite the demonstration objects that later steps use.

    Row Item Upper Pitt River Challenge
    1 Data 1948-2021, 74 years, spawners 2.1 to 74.6 thousand; S_new = 5.3 thousand spawners (average of 2018-2021) E01.C2, E03.C5
    2 Fits usable four checks TRUE for the Ricker, the random walk, Beverton-Holt and Ricker + NPGO E04.C4, E06.C3, E09.C4

    5 Residuals Ricker lag-1 0.47 against a limit of 0.23, long waves over time, QQ plot bends below the line at both ends; random walk lag-1 0.13 E07.C2
    6 Simulation observed lag-1 0.58: reached by 0 of 200 Ricker simulations and 62.5% of random-walk simulations; self-test of the walk: 30 of 30 refits pass, no sd_walk at zero E08.C5

    8 Forecast skill hindcast from 2007: Ricker skill 0.78, bias +0.74, coverage 0.67; random walk skill 0.82, bias 0.00, coverage 0.60; benchmark coverage 0.40. AIC and the hindcast disagree E11.C4

    Building the Lesson

    • Each episode is knitted in a fresh R session. Episodes 1 and 2 load the data themselves, and Episodes 3 to 11 start with a Starting Point chunk that recreates everything they need. The capstone runs no code: its template and solutions are shown, not run.
    • episodes/files/cookbook.R must stay identical to the code taught in the episodes. If you change a recipe, change it in both places, and in every episode that uses it.
    • config.yaml sets fail_on_error: true, so any unplanned error stops the build. Chunks that are meant to fail are marked error=TRUE.
    • No chunk takes more than about 5 seconds. The slowest is the optional profile interval in Episode 10; the 50-simulation self-test in Episode 8 takes about 2 seconds.
    • Run sandpaper::validate_lesson(headings = TRUE) before you commit. The README explains how to build the lesson locally.

    A Private Repository

    • GitHub Pages can serve a site from a private repository only on a paid GitHub plan, and the site may still be public.
    • Until the lesson is ready to share, build it locally and share the site/docs/ folder as a zip file.
